name: Hana Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Hana, thanks for joining. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to tech companies, employers, unions or government, and everything you tell me is confidential. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the acute medical unit, which is where people go straight from the emergency department for the first two days. It's fast: I might admit four people and discharge three in a shift, chest pains, strokes, infections, people who've just collapsed at home. I take the history, sort the bloods, start the drips and try to make sense of the chaos before the doctors' round.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what tires you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the speed and the detective work, working out what's going on with someone who arrived ten minutes ago. What tires me out is the admin per admission, which is like twenty screens. I use AI every day outside work, and I've built myself a little shift-swap tracker with it that half the unit now uses.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a house with two friends from uni, and I've saved hard, so I've got about a year and a half of pay between savings and a small share portfolio. I also do paid testing for a health-tech start-up a few evenings a month, checking whether their triage chatbot gives safe advice. I'm single, and I like having options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first one is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Huh. I'd be surprised, but okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was oversold, but the small stuff still helps. At work I'd keep showing people the little shortcuts. Online I'd post a fairly balanced take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. My job doesn't change, my pay's good and I'd have savings. The start-up testing gig might dry up, but that's pocket money, not rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the unit and keep improving the shift-swap tracker. I'd keep doing the start-up testing while it lasts. I'd probably apply for the advanced clinical practitioner training in the next year, which is about examining and prescribing like a junior doctor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly let down, but not bothered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which routine task would you most want a machine to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The admission paperwork. Every patient who arrives on the acute unit costs me twenty minutes of clicking before I've even touched them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the start-up gig might dry up. Would you miss it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The money, a little. More the feeling of being early on something. But I'd find another side project, I always do.

say: I'd say AI was **oversold**, but small things still help.
I'd keep sharing **shortcuts** at work and post a **balanced** take online.
think: I think I'd be **fine**, with good pay and **savings** behind me.
The **start-up gig** might dry up, but that's pocket money, not rent.
do: Keep improving my **shift-swap tracker** for the unit.
Keep **testing** the start-up's triage chatbot while the work lasts.
Apply for **advanced practitioner** training in the next year.
feel: **Calm**, slightly let down but not bothered.
S0.quote: Every patient who arrives on the acute unit costs me twenty minutes of clicking before I've even touched them.
fieldNote: She is **secure** on every front, so the plateau barely touches her.
Her **side work** testing a triage chatbot is unusual for a ward nurse.
She talks about **options**, a word that recurs and fits her adaptive style.

steps.text: Apply for the advanced clinical practitioner training programme
Keep testing the start-up's triage chatbot a few evenings monthly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one feels right to me. It's basically already happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mostly good for nurses if we're involved early. At work I'd be the one showing colleagues how to use the new tools. Online I'd be sharing what's working on our unit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's great for me. I'm already fast with the tools, and the unit will need someone who can bridge the IT team and the nurses. The risk is the people who won't learn, and the managers who'll use it to cut corners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to be the unit's digital champion right away and run the training sessions. I'd still go for the advanced practitioner training. I'd also try to turn my testing gig into a paid advisory role with one or two health-tech firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and honestly excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned people who won't learn. Who?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A couple of the older nurses, and one or two my age, actually. The nurses who refuse the new systems won't lose their jobs, but they'll be the ones stuck on bed baths while the rest of us run the unit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got a few things on. Are you spreading yourself thin?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But that's how I like it. If one thing stalls, the others keep going.

say: I'd say AI is good for nurses if they're **involved early**.
I'd share online what's **working** on our unit.
think: I think it's **great for me**, being fast with the tools already.
The risk is **managers cutting corners** and colleagues who won't learn.
do: Volunteer as the unit's **digital champion** and run training sessions.
Turn the testing gig into **paid advisory** work for health-tech firms.
S1.quote: The nurses who refuse the new systems won't lose their jobs, but they'll be the ones stuck on bed baths while the rest of us run the unit.
fieldNote: She sees Steady Disruption as a clear **opportunity** for herself.
She's blunt that **refusers** will be sidelined to the least wanted tasks.
Her habit of **many projects** is her way of managing risk.

steps.text: Sign up as the acute unit's digital champion
Start the advanced clinical practitioner course
Pitch paid advisory work to two health-tech firms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Whoa. Okay, let me think about that properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need sensible rules quickly, so hospitals don't just buy whatever's cheapest. At work I'd tell people to get good at the tools now. Online I'd try to be calm and useful, not scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it shakes my plan. The advanced practitioner job is all thinking work, diagnosing and prescribing, so AGI in 2028 does that before I'd even finish training. My hands-on nursing actually looks safer, until 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pause the advanced practitioner course, because it'd be outdated. I'd go hard on the health-tech side, because the firms building this will need nurses to make it safe. I'd put more of my savings into shares in those firms, carefully, maybe a fifth of what I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but buzzing. Like the floor's moving, but I can see where to step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap between thinking AI and robots mean for your work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On my unit, half the job is thinking and half is hands. The more senior I get in nursing, the more of my job is thinking work, so fast AGI hits my career plan before it hits my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd put a fifth of your savings into shares. Isn't that a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I'd keep the rest in cash. But if the whole economy is going to run on these firms, holding none of them feels riskier.

say: I'd call for **sensible rules** so hospitals don't buy the **cheapest** systems.
I'd tell colleagues to get good at the **tools** now, staying calm online.
think: Advanced practice is **thinking work**, so AGI beats it before I finish training.
My **hands-on** nursing looks safer, but only until **2031**.
do: **Pause** the advanced practitioner course as likely outdated.
Push into **health-tech** work making AI safe for patients.
Move about **a fifth** of my savings into shares in AI firms.
feel: **Anxious** but buzzing, as if she can see where to step.
S2.quote: The more senior I get in nursing, the more of my job is thinking work, so fast AGI hits my career plan before it hits my hands.
fieldNote: Fast AGI **reverses** her career plan: senior thinking roles become the risky ones.
She'd **invest** in the firms causing the disruption, as a hedge.
Her anxiety comes with **energy** rather than dread.

steps.text: Pause the advanced clinical practitioner course
Apply for a part-time clinical safety role at a health-tech firm
Move a fifth of savings into shares of AI companies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a better runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the five years are for getting nurses ready, so hospitals should start training now. I'd say that loudly at work. Online I'd share practical stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I can finish advanced practice and use it for a few years. But I'd aim for a hybrid role, part clinical, part overseeing AI tools, because pure diagnosis isn't safe past 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the advanced practitioner training by 2029, then move toward a clinical safety lead role. I'd grow the health-tech advisory work into something real. I'd invest a bit more, but slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly focused.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a hybrid role look like day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half on the unit, half checking the AI's admission decisions and training staff on it. I want to be the nurse who checks the AI's diagnosis, not the nurse whose diagnosis the AI checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would any of this change where you live?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. There are big hospitals and the tech firms all within an hour. That's one reason I'm calm-ish.

say: I'd say the **five years** should go into getting **nurses ready**.
I'd say this **loudly at work** and share practical tips online.
think: I could finish **advanced practice** and use it for a few years.
I'd aim for a **hybrid role**, as pure diagnosis isn't safe past 2031.
do: Move toward a **clinical safety lead** role overseeing AI tools.
Grow the **advisory work** and invest a bit more, slowly.
S3.quote: I want to be the nurse who checks the AI's diagnosis, not the nurse whose diagnosis the AI checks.
fieldNote: Five years lets her **keep** the advanced practice plan, with a hybrid twist.
Having **hospitals and tech firms** nearby keeps her settled.
She frames her goal as **checking** the AI rather than being checked by it.

steps.text: Finish advanced clinical practitioner training by 2029
Apply for a clinical safety lead role overseeing AI admissions
Grow health-tech advisory work to one paid day a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, as long as people actually use it. I'd say it to colleagues who think it'll never happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be excited. I'd get a full advanced practice career in, plus a move into leadership or tech by the late 2030s. With a decade's warning, I'd stop worrying about robots and start worrying about which of my side projects to drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Advanced practitioner training over the next two years, then use it properly for a good while. Keep the advisory work going on the side. Keep investing steadily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and quite optimistic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave nursing by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not fully. I'd want to keep a hand in, maybe one clinical day a week. It keeps you honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell colleagues who think it'll never happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That ten years is the same as two if you ignore it for nine. I'd show them what the tools can already do.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty**, as long as people **use it**.
I'd tell **doubting colleagues** that ignoring it wastes the time.
think: I'd be **excited**, with a full advanced practice career ahead.
I'd plan a move into **leadership or tech** by the late 2030s.
do: Complete **advanced practitioner** training over two years.
Keep the **advisory work** going on the side.
S4.quote: With a decade's warning, I'd stop worrying about robots and start worrying about which of my side projects to drop.
fieldNote: A decade makes this a **career strategy** question for her, not a threat.
She'd keep **one clinical day** a week even after moving on.
Her worry shifts to **too many options**, a sign of real security.

steps.text: Complete advanced clinical practitioner training by 2028
Keep paid advisory work with health-tech firms on the side

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it flips my career plan; the higher I climb, the faster I'm replaced. Fast AGI would turn every promotion I've worked for into a quicker route to being replaced. What would help is hospitals bringing nurses in to design how the tools get used, and flexible training that doesn't take years.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether nurses get paid for testing this stuff. The firms need us, and right now most nurses do it for free in pilot schemes.

headlineQuote: Fast AGI would turn every promotion I've worked for into a quicker route to being replaced.
portrait: Hana is a **27-year-old** acute medical unit nurse who uses **AI daily** and built her unit's shift-swap tracker.
She shares a house, has **eighteen months** of savings and shares, and does paid **chatbot testing**.
She's **calm** in slow worlds, seeing them as chances to climb into advanced practice.
AGI by 2028 makes her **anxious**, because senior nursing roles are mostly thinking work.
She hedges with **side work** and investing, and talks constantly about keeping options.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, which turns her **promotion path** into faster replacement.
whatWouldHelp: Hospitals involving **nurses in designing** how AI tools are used.
**Short, flexible** training that doesn't take years.
